title: Drinking Before a Blood Test: How Long to Stop and Why
excerpt: Can you drink alcohol before a blood test? How long to stop, whether alcohol breaks a fast, which results it can affect, and what to do if you already drank.
metaDescription: Can you drink before a blood test? How long to stop, whether alcohol breaks a fast, which results it affects, and what to do if you already drank.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for most routine blood tests, the safest plan is to skip alcohol for at least 24 hours beforehand, and longer (often 48 to 72 hours) if you're having liver tests or a cholesterol panel, or if your doctor or lab says so. If the test requires fasting, alcohol counts as breaking the fast, so the night before should be water only. A drink or two a couple of days earlier usually won't change much, but a big night out the evening before can push several common results in the wrong direction and lead to repeat tests or confusing follow-up conversations. Whatever you drank, tell the person drawing your blood or your doctor. That information helps them read your results correctly.

**The quick rules:** Follow your lab's or doctor's instructions first, because they know exactly which tests are ordered. If you have no specific instructions, avoid alcohol for 24 hours before any blood test, and aim for 48 to 72 hours before a liver panel or lipid (cholesterol) panel. For a fasting test, have nothing but plain water for the stated window, usually 8 to 12 hours. Drink plenty of water so the draw is easier. If you already drank, don't panic and don't lie about it. Mention it, and ask whether the test should go ahead or be rescheduled.

> **This is not medical advice.** This guide explains general preparation guidance. It does not interpret any test result, and it is not a substitute for instructions from your doctor or the lab running your test. **Talk to your doctor if** you take medication for diabetes (alcohol plus fasting can drop your blood sugar), you've been told your liver enzymes, triglycerides, or blood sugar were abnormal before, you're unsure whether your test requires fasting, or your test is for a specific medical, legal, or workplace reason. **Get urgent care** if you feel shaky, sweaty, confused, or faint while fasting after drinking, since those can be signs of low blood sugar. In an emergency, call 911.

## Can You Drink Alcohol Before a Blood Test?

You can, in the sense that nothing dangerous usually happens if you have a glass of wine two days before a routine check-up. But "can" isn't the useful question. The useful question is whether the alcohol will change your results enough to matter, and for some tests it can.

Blood tests are snapshots. They show what's in your blood at one moment and compare it with ranges taken from large groups of people. Most of those reference ranges assume a fairly ordinary state: not freshly sick, not just back from a marathon, not hungover. Alcohol is one of the most common things that moves people away from that ordinary state, because the body treats it as a priority to clear. While your liver is busy with alcohol, it temporarily changes how it handles fats, sugar, and other substances, and those changes show up in the blood.

That's why many lab and clinic instructions ask patients to avoid alcohol for at least 24 hours before a test. Some ask for longer. The exact wording varies by lab, and there is no single universal rule that every lab uses. If yours gave you a number, use theirs.

## How Long Before a Blood Test Should You Stop Drinking?

There isn't one official waiting period for every test. Here's a practical guide based on the kinds of instructions labs commonly give and on how alcohol affects each type of result. It is general guidance, not a rule from any one lab.

| Test type | Common prep advice on alcohol | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Routine blood count (CBC), most general panels | Avoid for at least 24 hours | Heavy drinking can cause dehydration, which can concentrate some values |
| Fasting blood sugar or glucose tolerance test | No alcohol during the fasting window; many advise 24 hours or more | Alcohol can lower or raise blood sugar and breaks the fast |
| Lipid (cholesterol) panel | Avoid for 24 hours at minimum; 48 to 72 hours is often suggested | Alcohol can raise triglycerides for some time after drinking |
| Liver function tests (ALT, AST, GGT, bilirubin) | Avoid for at least 24 hours; longer is better, and your doctor may want to know about recent heavy drinking | Alcohol is processed by the liver, and some markers respond to it |
| Uric acid (often checked for gout) | Avoid for 24 to 48 hours | Alcohol can raise uric acid levels |
| Tests specifically looking for alcohol use | Follow the instructions given | These are designed to detect drinking, not to be prepared for |

Two things are worth saying plainly. First, a 24-hour gap after a light drink is very different from a 24-hour gap after six or eight drinks. Your body clears alcohol at roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot between people, so a heavy night can mean alcohol is still being processed well into the next day, and its effects on fats and blood sugar can last longer. Our guide on [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explains the timing in more detail.

Second, no short break will "reset" results that reflect a long-term pattern. If you drink heavily most days, stopping for two days before a test won't hide that from certain markers, and that isn't the point of preparing anyway. The point is to make sure one recent night out doesn't distort a picture that's supposed to reflect your normal health.

## Does Alcohol Count as Breaking a Fast for a Blood Test?

Yes. When a test requires fasting, labs typically mean no food and no drinks other than plain water for the stated period, usually 8 to 12 hours. Alcohol is not allowed during that window. It contains calories, it is processed by the liver, and it can change blood sugar and blood fats, which are exactly the things fasting tests are trying to measure cleanly.

The common fasting tests are:

- **Fasting blood glucose**, used to check blood sugar control
- **Glucose tolerance tests**, where you drink a sugar solution and have blood drawn over a couple of hours
- **Lipid panels**, though many doctors now order non-fasting cholesterol tests, so check whether yours needs fasting
- **Some metabolic panels and specific tests your doctor may order**

If you're unsure whether your test is a fasting one, call the lab or check your order. Showing up fasted when you didn't need to is a minor inconvenience. Showing up after a few glasses of wine when you did need to fast can mean doing the whole thing again.

### What you can drink while fasting

Plain water is fine and usually encouraged. Black coffee, tea, flavored water, sparkling drinks, juice, and sports drinks are often not allowed during a fasting window, though instructions vary. When in doubt, stick to water.

### A warning for people on diabetes medication

Fasting after drinking can lower blood sugar. Alcohol interferes with the liver's ability to release stored sugar into the blood, and when you also haven't eaten for 8 to 12 hours, that effect can be stronger. For people taking insulin or certain diabetes tablets, the combination can cause a low that sneaks up quickly. If you take diabetes medication, ask your doctor how to handle fasting and alcohol before your test, and don't drink the night before a fasting draw. For more on this, see our guide on [alcohol and blood sugar management](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025).

## Which Blood Tests Can Alcohol Affect?

This section explains which tests are sensitive to alcohol in general terms. It doesn't tell you what any particular number means for you. Your doctor interprets results alongside your history, other tests, and how you feel.

### Cholesterol and triglycerides (lipid panel)

A lipid panel usually reports total cholesterol, LDL ("bad") cholesterol, HDL ("good") cholesterol, and triglycerides. Of these, **triglycerides** are the most sensitive to alcohol. Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood, and drinking alcohol can raise them for some hours after you drink, especially when combined with a heavy, fatty meal. Some people are more prone to this than others.

That matters because a high triglyceride result can affect how the rest of the panel is calculated and interpreted. In many labs, LDL cholesterol is estimated from the other numbers rather than measured directly, and very high triglycerides can make that estimate less reliable. A big night out before a lipid test can therefore produce a result that doesn't reflect your usual state.

Regular drinking also has longer-term effects on cholesterol, which is a separate topic from test prep. We cover that in our guide on [whether alcohol raises cholesterol](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-raise-cholesterol).

### Liver function tests

Liver panels typically include enzymes called **ALT**, **AST**, **ALP**, and **GGT**, plus bilirubin and proteins such as albumin. These are among the tests people worry about most when they've been drinking.

In plain terms:

- **GGT** is an enzyme that tends to rise with regular, heavier drinking. It doesn't usually jump after a single night for most people, but it reflects patterns over recent weeks. Because it can take weeks to come back down after drinking is cut back, a couple of dry days won't change it much.
- **ALT and AST** are enzymes released when liver cells are stressed or damaged. Many things can raise them, including alcohol, some medicines, fatty liver, viral hepatitis, and even hard exercise in the days before a test (AST is also found in muscle).
- **Bilirubin and proteins** reflect other aspects of liver function and are influenced by many factors.

A single drink a day or two before a liver test is unlikely to be the main story for most people. But heavy drinking in the days before the test can affect some markers, and regular heavy drinking affects them more. If you're having liver tests, the most helpful thing is to avoid alcohol beforehand and tell your doctor honestly how much you usually drink. They'll interpret the results with that in mind. For background on how the liver handles alcohol, see [how alcohol is metabolized](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-is-metabolized).

### Blood sugar (glucose and HbA1c)

Alcohol can push blood sugar in either direction. Sugary drinks, mixers, and cocktails can raise it, while alcohol itself can lower it by slowing the liver's release of stored sugar, especially when you haven't eaten. A fasting glucose taken the morning after drinking may not reflect your usual fasting level.

**HbA1c** is different. It reflects average blood sugar over roughly the past two to three months, so one night of drinking won't meaningfully change it. That's one reason doctors use it alongside fasting glucose.

### Uric acid

Uric acid is often checked when someone has symptoms of gout or as part of a broader panel. Alcohol, and beer in particular, can raise uric acid levels, partly because the body's handling of alcohol makes it harder for the kidneys to clear uric acid. Avoiding alcohol for a day or two before a uric acid test helps keep the result representative.

### Complete blood count (CBC)

A CBC measures red cells, white cells, and platelets. One night of drinking usually doesn't change it much, but dehydration from heavy drinking can make the blood slightly more concentrated, which can nudge some values. Longer-term heavy drinking is associated with changes such as larger red blood cells (a higher **MCV**), but that reflects months of drinking, not last weekend. Red blood cells live for around four months, so this kind of change can't be undone with a short break.

### Kidney function and electrolytes

Tests like creatinine, urea (BUN), sodium, and potassium can be affected by dehydration. Alcohol makes you pee more, and if you also sweated, vomited, or didn't drink much water, your kidney numbers can look a bit off temporarily. Drinking water before your test helps here as well.

## Having a Blood Test While Hungover

If you wake up hungover on test day, the honest move is to tell the lab or your doctor and ask whether to go ahead. Many routine tests will be fine. Fasting tests, lipid panels, and liver panels are the ones most likely to be worth rescheduling, especially if the night before was heavy.

A few practical points if you do go:

- **Hydrate.** Drink a couple of glasses of plain water before your appointment. Being well hydrated makes veins easier to find, which can make the draw quicker and less uncomfortable.
- **Expect to feel worse than usual during the draw.** Dehydration, low blood sugar, and a lingering hangover make some people more likely to feel lightheaded or faint during blood draws. Tell the phlebotomist (the person drawing blood) if you feel off, and ask to lie down if you have a history of fainting.
- **Eat after the draw.** If you were fasting, bring a snack for afterward.
- **Don't take extra painkillers "for the test."** Some medicines can also affect results, and alcohol plus a hangover is a common time for people to over-use pain relievers.

If you're dealing with nausea or a pounding head on the morning of a test, our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) can help you plan how much time to give yourself.

## Tests That Look for Alcohol Specifically

Some blood tests aren't affected by alcohol by accident. They're designed to detect it. These are used in medical care, workplace testing, legal settings, and transplant programs. The common ones are:

- **Blood alcohol concentration (BAC):** measures alcohol currently in the blood. It only reflects recent drinking, usually within hours.
- **PEth (phosphatidylethanol):** forms in red blood cells only when alcohol is present. It can reflect drinking over the previous few weeks and is considered quite specific to alcohol.
- **CDT (carbohydrate-deficient transferrin):** tends to rise with sustained heavier drinking over a period of weeks.
- **GGT and MCV:** sometimes used as supporting markers, though many things other than alcohol can change them.

If you've been asked to take one of these tests, follow the instructions you were given. These tests exist to measure drinking, and there's no prep that makes them "pass" other than not drinking. Trying to game them isn't worth it, and you should be truthful with whoever ordered the test. For a detailed explanation of how these markers differ, see our guide to [PEth vs EtG alcohol testing](/never-hungover/peth-vs-etg-alcohol-testing-advanced-biomarker-comparison-guide-2025).

## What About Medications, Supplements, and Other Prep?

Alcohol is just one thing that can shift results. While you're preparing, it's worth checking a few others:

- **Medications:** Keep taking prescribed medicines unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Some tests have specific instructions, such as timing a thyroid pill around the draw. Ask if you're unsure.
- **Supplements:** High-dose biotin (often found in hair, skin, and nail supplements) is known to interfere with some lab tests, including certain thyroid and heart tests. The FDA has warned about this. Tell your doctor about any supplements you take, and ask whether to pause them before your test.
- **Hard exercise:** A tough workout in the day or two before a test can raise muscle-related markers, including AST and CK.
- **Smoking and caffeine:** Some labs ask you to avoid these before certain tests, especially fasting ones.
- **Being unwell:** A recent cold, infection, or injury can affect results like white cell counts and inflammation markers. Mention it.

## How to Prepare: A Simple Checklist

Here's a straightforward plan for most routine blood tests:

1. **Read your instructions.** Check whether the test requires fasting and whether the lab gave a specific alcohol rule.
2. **Skip alcohol for at least 24 hours,** and 48 to 72 hours if you're having a lipid panel or liver tests, or if your doctor suggests it.
3. **If fasting, stop eating and drinking anything except water** at the time you were given, usually 8 to 12 hours before the draw.
4. **Drink water** the evening before and the morning of the test.
5. **Get a normal night of sleep** and avoid unusually hard exercise the day before.
6. **List your medications and supplements,** including anything you take occasionally.
7. **Tell the truth about drinking.** Your doctor isn't judging you. They need accurate information to interpret your results and avoid ordering unnecessary follow-up tests.

## What If You Already Drank?

It happens, especially when a test gets booked around a weekend or a celebration. Here's what to do:

- **One or two drinks more than 24 hours ago:** For most routine tests, this is unlikely to matter much. Mention it anyway.
- **Several drinks within the last 24 hours, or a heavy night before a fasting, lipid, or liver test:** Call the lab or your doctor's office and ask whether to reschedule. Rebooking is usually easy, and it's better than getting a result that leads to worry or repeat testing.
- **You're not sure:** Go, tell them exactly what you drank and when, and let the clinician decide. They can note it alongside your results.

What you shouldn't do is hide it. If a result comes back unusual and your doctor doesn't know you'd been drinking, they may order more tests or start a conversation about a problem that doesn't exist.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Take extra care with alcohol before a blood test if you:

- Take **insulin or other diabetes medication**, since alcohol plus fasting can lower blood sugar
- Have been told before that your **liver enzymes, triglycerides, or blood sugar** were high
- Have **gout** or are being tested for it
- Are being tested for a **specific medical decision**, such as starting a medication, checking a treatment, or before surgery
- Drink **regularly or heavily**, in which case the most useful thing is an honest conversation with your doctor about your usual intake

## The Bigger Picture: Your Results Reflect Your Habits

Short-term prep matters, but blood tests are most useful when they show your normal state. If your usual week includes a lot of drinking, a few dry days before the test won't change long-term markers, and that's actually useful information for your doctor. Many people find that cutting back for a few weeks before a planned check-up and then talking openly about their drinking leads to a more productive appointment.

If you're trying to drink more comfortably day to day, the most effective steps are the simple ones: drink less, drink slower, eat beforehand, and alternate alcoholic drinks with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also use supplements around drinking. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's best described as promising rather than proven. It will not change your blood test results, it isn't a way to prepare for a test, and you should mention it to your doctor like any other supplement. If you want to try it for nights out, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Follow your lab's or doctor's instructions first. They know which tests are ordered.
- Without specific instructions, avoid alcohol for at least 24 hours before a blood test, and 48 to 72 hours before a lipid panel or liver tests.
- Alcohol breaks a fast. For fasting tests, have only plain water during the fasting window.
- Triglycerides, blood sugar, uric acid, and some liver markers are the results most likely to be affected by recent drinking.
- Long-term markers like GGT, MCV, HbA1c, PEth, and CDT reflect weeks or months, not one night, and a short break won't change them.
- If you already drank, tell the lab or your doctor and ask whether to reschedule. Never hide it.
- If you take diabetes medication, ask your doctor before fasting and avoid drinking the night before.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can I drink alcohol the night before a blood test?**

It's best not to. Most labs and clinics advise avoiding alcohol for at least 24 hours before a blood test, and some ask for longer before cholesterol or liver tests. If your test requires fasting, alcohol counts as breaking the fast. If you already drank, tell the lab or your doctor and ask whether to go ahead or reschedule.

**How long before a blood test should I stop drinking alcohol?**

There's no single rule for every test, so follow your lab's instructions first. As a general guide, avoid alcohol for at least 24 hours before routine blood work and aim for 48 to 72 hours before a lipid panel or liver function tests. After a heavy night, give yourself more time, since alcohol can take well into the next day to clear and its effects on blood fats and sugar can last longer.

**Does alcohol break a fast for a blood test?**

Yes. Fasting for a blood test usually means no food or drinks except plain water for 8 to 12 hours. Alcohol contains calories, is processed by the liver, and can change blood sugar and triglycerides, so it isn't allowed during the fasting window. Water is fine and usually encouraged.

**Will one drink affect my blood test results?**

One drink more than a day before a routine test is unlikely to change most results much. Closer to the test, or before a fasting, cholesterol, or liver test, even modest drinking can affect results like triglycerides and blood sugar. The simplest approach is to skip alcohol beforehand and mention any recent drinking to your doctor.

**Can alcohol affect a cholesterol test?**

Yes, mainly through triglycerides. Drinking can raise triglyceride levels for some hours afterward, especially alongside a heavy meal, and very high triglycerides can make the calculated LDL cholesterol less reliable. Avoid alcohol for at least 24 hours, and ideally 48 to 72 hours, before a lipid panel.

**Will drinking show up on a liver function test?**

It depends on how much and how often. A single drink a day or two earlier is unlikely to be the main factor for most people, but heavy drinking in the days before a test can affect some markers, and regular heavy drinking affects them more. GGT in particular reflects recent weeks of drinking and won't drop after a couple of dry days. Tell your doctor honestly how much you usually drink so they can interpret the results correctly.

**Is it okay to get blood drawn while hungover?**

For many routine tests it's fine, but fasting tests, cholesterol panels, and liver panels may be worth rescheduling after a heavy night. Tell the lab you've been drinking and ask. Drink water beforehand, and let the person drawing blood know if you feel lightheaded, since dehydration and low blood sugar make fainting more likely.

**Can a blood test tell if you've been drinking?**

Some can. A blood alcohol test shows alcohol in the blood within recent hours. Tests like PEth and CDT are designed to detect drinking over the past few weeks, and markers like GGT and MCV can be associated with longer-term heavy drinking. Routine blood work isn't designed to detect drinking, but some results may prompt your doctor to ask about it.
